text:
Why I Wasn't Surprised by Tuesday's Election
I've been an election worker since 2018. I started as a cross-trained clerk, and I loved it from day one.
I became an election worker because I wanted to serve my country. My dad served in the military and fought in the Vietnam War because he loved this nation and was willing to serve it. I couldn't serve in the military because of my hearing loss, but I could serve as an election worker. It's not the same as military service, but it's something I can do to contribute to the nation I live in and love.
Over the years I've had the wonderful opportunity to get to know and work alongside people of all political backgrounds and beliefs, and I have never once had trouble with any of them. I worked my way up to Supervising Judge, which is a fancy way of saying I manage a polling place and its team. Following the law and our procedures has always mattered a great deal to me. For anyone who doesn't know: in Kansas, we check every voter's photo ID.
Many people are surprised by Tuesday's results and the Democrats' huge win. I'm not. I don't like the results, but I'm not blindsided.
And let's be clear: Kansas didn't lose its conservative values just because it voted for Democrats. On the same ballot, Kansans voted YES, roughly 64% to 36%, on a constitutional amendment stating that only U.S. citizens can vote in our elections.
Being an election worker lets me see voter behavior firsthand. After serving thousands of voters over the years, and more than 1,000 on Tuesday alone, here's what I want people to understand: we are more united than divided. The news, social media, and certain podcasters love to show division. But when you actually get out there and serve, you find that most people have common sense. There are nuances and small differences here and there, but the basics are mostly the same.
Sure, there are the extreme one-offs that make you wonder what on earth happened to humanity. On Tuesday, more than 1,000 voters came through my polling place, and exactly one gave me grief about my team following the procedures the law requires. Do I write off the whole day because of that one voter? Of course not! We had a very successful day. It's the same with society. There are people out there doing violent things, but that doesn't write off the rest of us.
So here's my observation of why Republicans lost.
1. They depended too much on brand loyalty.
That worked for Boomers and older generations. They could work for one company until they retired. They found a brand they liked and stuck with it for life, no matter how bad it got or how often it changed the recipe. That doesn't work for Gen X, Millennials, and younger generations. We've had to change jobs every so often, because loyalty to a company can cost you money. So we won't stay with a political party that betrays the American people. Republicans were elected to secure the border, secure our elections, cut spending, end endless wars abroad, and release the Epstein files. Loyalty has to be earned, not just given.
2. People rebel when they're called names.
Remember when Trump first ran, and the left called Republicans all kinds of names? Even people in the center got called names, and many of them decided to vote for Trump. This time around, I've seen more and more people on the right calling the left names just as bad. I'm not saying the left doesn't do it. They have, and worse. Some on the left have even said they want to kill those on the right. But lowering our standards to theirs won't win more hearts and minds.
3. Propaganda.
When I was a kid, a teacher told me to always be aware of propaganda. (Naturally, this was before the sweeping changes in public education.) I've never forgotten that warning, and I've always taken ads, especially political ones, with a grain of salt.
Just look at the ads in the Kansas Senate race between Roger Marshall and Adam Hamilton. Both sides slung mud and twisted the truth. It came across as lazy and shameful. Whatever happened to showing your constituents how you've voted on their behalf, what you've accomplished, and what your goals are for the next term?
Most people don't have time to dissect an ad, let alone suspect that what it says about the other side might be wrong. Some will say there's no excuse, since a quick internet search or an AI summary can tell you what really happened. But most people don't want to do that. When an ad sounds bogus, that's how people take it. When it sounds realistic and touches what viewers experience in real life, who do you think they'll believe? It doesn't matter to them whether it's factual. If an ad offers a reason why gas costs more, or why students are graduating high school reading at a third-grade level, they'll go with that over the ad calling the opponent an extremist, a pedophile, or a communist. What moves voters most is what affects their own lives.
4. Democrats organize and pivot.
One thing Democrats have done well is organize quickly in unity and pivot whenever they need to. They learned early to reach younger generations. They infiltrated schools and indoctrinated the younger generation. Don't believe me? Look at some of the lessons being taught. Students aren't being taught how to think; they're being taught what to think. By the time they reach college, their mindset is completely socialist.
And instead of addressing the actual problem, which is the level of expectations, we blame teachers who are only doing the jobs they're expected to do. We pile on more responsibilities and take away their ability to manage their classrooms. Then we wonder why so many teachers, even those with years of experience, quit before they can retire.
Where do we go from here?
I know the United States can survive. As Ezra Taft Benson said in 1986: "I have faith that the Constitution will be saved as prophesied by Joseph Smith. But it will not be saved in Washington. It will be saved by the citizens of this nation who love and cherish freedom. It will be saved by enlightened members of this Church—men and women who will subscribe to and abide by the principles of the Constitution."
It won't be saved in Washington. It will be saved at your kitchen table, and in how you treat other people. Put down your phone, get out, and serve your community. Get to know your neighbors and talk with them.
And Republicans need to understand this: voters aren't going to vote for you just because you say the other guy is the bad guy, when you're doing the bad-guy stuff yourself!

The technical transfer itself is real

The Royal Artillery Museum identifies Mysorean rockets as the inspiration for Congreve’s British military rockets and records that captured examples were sent to Britain for development at Woolwich.”

“MI5’s institutional history dates the Secret Service Bureau to 1909, in the context of concerns about German espionage. The documented British contribution to the creation of the American OSS runs through William Donovan’s wartime contacts and British assistance in 1940–1941.”

“Frankfurt’s municipal chronicle records the cornerstone ceremony for Battelle’s German laboratory on October 31, 1952. That corrects the October 28 date in my progress update. The site was on Wiesbadener Straße, on the former Rebstock airfield. 

The same entry says the buildings and facilities were financed entirely from the foundation established by Gordon Battelle’s estate.

For your investigation, this supplies a concrete institutional connection between Battelle and postwar Frankfurt, close in time to the institute’s documented intelligence-related work.”

“The CIA’s 1953 record names Battelle

The key document is Frederick C. Durant’s February 16, 1953 report on the CIA-sponsored scientific panel chaired by Howard P. Robertson.

Its account of the January 15 meeting states that J. Allen Hynek described Battelle’s Project STORK support. Edward J. Ruppelt was also present, briefing the panel on the Air Technical Intelligence Center’s collection and analysis procedures. The report places this work within the CIA’s Office of Scientific Intelligence review of UFO reports. 

The directly relevant names are therefore Hynek, Ruppelt, Durant, Robertson, and H. Marshall Chadwell, rather than only the better-known Dulles and Harriman figures. These are the people in the operational and scientific records nearest Battelle’s documented role. 

This establishes Battelle → Air Force technical intelligence → CIA scientific assessment. The record concerns evaluation of reports; it does not establish possession of extraordinary aircraft or materials.

There is also a personnel connection independent of the UFO investigation

The Science History Institute’s oral history with Madeline M. Henderson supplies another route.

Henderson describes working with James W. Perry and Allen Kent on scientific information retrieval. Their work attracted Joseph Becker at the CIA; she recalls personal-service contracts with the Agency and work associated with MIT’s Center for International Studies. She dates her move to Battelle to July 1, 1953. 

Their interests included making information about people, places, organizations, and technical subjects retrievable across documents. Her account distinguishes the earlier CIA assignment from the later Battelle work, including a Battelle contract at Aberdeen Proving Ground. …”

🇺🇲 NYT | Inside the Republican collapse: How Trump's Iran war, economic failures and strategic miscalculations handed Democrats a historic midterm victory

Six days before Americans went to the polls, Donald Trump's senior political strategists gathered for a private video conference. The conversation began with a joke about cyanide pills.

What followed was a grim assessment of a political disaster that some of the president's closest advisers had been anticipating for months.

According to an extensive New York Times investigation by Shane Goldmacher and Jonathan Swan, based on interviews with more than 70 people involved in the elections, the Republican collapse was neither sudden nor entirely unexpected.

Internal polling had repeatedly warned that Trump's war against Iran, the economic consequences of the conflict and the president's deteriorating standing with voters were creating the conditions for a historic defeat.

By Tuesday night, Democrats had captured both chambers of Congress, winning Republican strongholds that had appeared virtually unreachable a year earlier.

The Times estimates that Republicans are on course to lose the national congressional popular vote by approximately 13 percentage points, potentially their worst midterm performance in half a century.

But the most consequential revelation concerns what Trump's own political operation knew about the war.

▫️ The warning from inside Trump's campaign

During the summer, James Blair, the strategist overseeing Trump's midterm operation, circulated a presentation to senior White House officials showing how Republican electoral fortunes were moving almost in parallel with developments in the Iran war.

When fighting intensified, Democrats' polling advantage expanded. During diplomatic negotiations, the gap narrowed. When the cease-fire collapsed, Democratic support surged again.

By late July, Democrats held a 10-point advantage on the generic congressional ballot.

The presentation contained an unmistakable warning: Republicans might retain the House if the Democratic advantage could be reduced to four points.

But that outcome depended on three conditions: a prolonged cease-fire, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and falling gasoline prices.

A Democratic advantage approaching 10 points, the document warned, would probably cost Republicans the Senate as well.

These were not retrospective explanations offered after an electoral defeat. They were warnings circulating inside the president's own political organization months before Election Day.

The administration nevertheless entered November with the war unresolved, Hormuz disrupted and American consumers facing sharply higher fuel prices.

The political consequences were visible long before the ballots were counted.

▫️ A war that transformed the election

Trump returned to the presidency promising to avoid new wars and bring down prices.

The conflict with Iran challenged both promises simultaneously.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted energy markets, pushing gasoline above $4 a gallon and contributing to a broader cost-of-living crisis. Diesel prices reached record highs, adding pressure to transportation, agriculture and the movement of goods.

The economic effects extended far beyond the battlefield.

For American households, the war became visible every time they filled their vehicles. For businesses, higher transportation and energy costs compounded the effects of Trump's tariffs.

According to the Times, Republican polling showed that voters who had supported the party but were considering staying home identified two priorities above all others: ending the war and addressing inflation.

Even Trump's own pollster, Tony Fabrizio, found that the MAGA Republican brand had become more unpopular than the democratic socialist label Republicans had spent months attacking.

The administration's political strategy had been built around portraying Democrats as the more extreme alternative.

The electorate's concerns had shifted toward the consequences of Republican governance.

Trump privately questioned the war's electoral cost

One of the report's most revealing passages concerns a question Trump reportedly asked before voting had even ended.

“If we never went into Iran, what do you think would happen in the midterms?”

The question suggests that the president was considering the electoral consequences of the conflict even before the full scale of the Republican defeat became clear.

Publicly, Trump has continued to defend the decision to attack Iran, arguing that preventing Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons justified the operation.

That distinction matters. Trump has acknowledged that the war may have damaged Republican electoral prospects without conceding that the military intervention itself was a mistake.

His administration is now debating whether to resume major combat operations, even as the incoming Democratic Congress prepares to challenge the war and its economic consequences.

▫️ The political damage extended beyond Iran

The Times describes a presidency whose problems accumulated across several fronts.

Trump's tariffs created difficulties for farmers and businesses, including in states Republicans had previously considered secure.

His administration faced repeated allegations involving conflicts of interest and the financial activities of his family and associates. The White House denied wrongdoing.

The administration's immigration enforcement campaign also became a political liability after two protesters were killed by federal agents in Minneapolis, incidents captured on video.

According to the reporting, Chief of Staff Susie Wiles had privately attempted to steer Trump away from the hard-line approach associated with Stephen Miller.

Democratic polling subsequently showed a shift in public attitudes toward immigration, an issue that had previously been among Trump's strongest electoral advantages.

Meanwhile, some of the president's own advisers were frustrated by his public priorities.

As voters struggled with inflation, Trump devoted attention to White House renovations, golf courses and other projects that advisers feared reinforced perceptions of indifference to economic hardship.

The cumulative effect was a political environment in which Republican candidates increasingly struggled to separate themselves from the president.

▫️How Trump's own decisions weakened the Republican map

The investigation also documents a series of strategic choices that expanded the party's vulnerabilities.

In North Carolina, Trump supported Michael Whatley, who ultimately lost to former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper.

In Texas, Trump backed Attorney General Ken Paxton over incumbent Republican Senator John Cornyn despite warnings that Paxton's controversies could endanger the seat.

Republicans eventually spent nearly $300 million defending Texas. Paxton lost by 12 points.

In South Carolina, Trump supported Darline Graham following the death of Senator Lindsey Graham. She lost in a state that had not elected a Democratic senator since 1998.

These defeats forced Republican organizations to divert resources away from traditional battlegrounds and toward states they had expected to win comfortably.

By the final weeks, party strategists were discussing emergency spending in South Carolina, Mississippi and other Republican strongholds.

The electoral map had expanded beyond the resources available to defend it.

▫️The redistricting strategy that failed

Trump had also sought to reshape the House battlefield through an aggressive mid-decade redistricting campaign.

The effort began in Texas, where Republicans created five additional districts designed to favor their candidates.

Democrats responded with their own redistricting initiatives and recruited candidates in districts Trump had carried by substantial margins.

The Times reports that Democratic strategists deliberately sought candidates with military, medical, agricultural and other professional backgrounds, emphasizing economic issues rather than ideological confrontation.

That approach allowed Democrats to compete in places that had been considered safely Republican.

In Kentucky's Sixth District, for example, military veteran and former federal prosecutor Zach Dembo won a district Trump had carried by 15 points.

Even several districts redesigned to protect Republican incumbents fell to Democrats.

The redistricting effort had failed to insulate the party from a national political shift.

▫️The Democrats prepared for an opportunity Republicans underestimated

The Times details how Democratic leaders spent much of 2025 recruiting candidates and preparing to contest a far broader electoral map.

Chuck Schumer persuaded former North Carolina Governor Roy Cooper and former Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown to run for the Senate. Both won.

House Democrats recruited candidates capable of competing in conservative districts and shifted resources away from defending some incumbents toward expanding the battlefield.

Their strategy emphasized economic affordability, corruption allegations and the consequences of the administration's policies.

Hakeem Jeffries told the Times that the Iran war had helped “supercharge” the contrast between the parties.

The Democrats' success was not simply the result of Republican mistakes. It also reflected organizational decisions made well before the political environment turned decisively against Trump.

▫️The final days: A campaign preparing for defeat

The private call six days before Election Day offers a revealing picture of the Republican leadership's expectations.

Fabrizio, Blair and other senior strategists joked about funeral arrangements, prison food, presidential pardons and the possibility of fleeing the country.

At one point, Blair sarcastically suggested that Netanyahu might protect them because Israel's prime minister had performed better in his own election.

The MAGA Inc. super PAC disputed the account, describing the reported quotations as fabricated gossip and defending its campaign investments.

But the Times' broader reporting describes a political operation that had been tracking its deteriorating position for months.

Republicans possessed enormous financial resources, an extensive campaign apparatus and the advantages of incumbency.

They could not reverse the damage from an unpopular president, an unresolved war and an economy that voters increasingly associated with the administration's decisions.

▫️What the defeat means for Trump's final two years

The election has fundamentally altered the institutional balance in Washington.

Democrats will control both the House and Senate when the new Congress convenes in January.

Jeffries is positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House, while Democratic leaders are preparing investigations into the administration's conduct, financial dealings and handling of the Iran war.

The consequences could extend into foreign policy. Trump's advisers are debating renewed military operations against Iran at the same time that congressional Democrats are preparing to challenge the administration's war strategy, spending decisions and tariff policies.

The New York Times investigation establishes that the political risks of the Iran conflict were recognized inside Trump's own operation months before the election.

The administration had been warned that its path to retaining congressional control depended heavily on ending the fighting, reopening Hormuz and bringing energy prices down.

None of those conditions had been secured by Election Day.

The result was a historic transfer of congressional power, driven by a combination of wartime economic pressure, dissatisfaction with the administration and Democratic organizational gains.

The coming confrontation between Trump and the new Congress will unfold against that record.

Source: The New York Times - Shane Goldmacher and Jonathan Swan. Reporting based on interviews with more than 70 officials, strategists, lawmakers and other participants in the 2026 midterm elections.

Russian documents Set out 'tectonic weapon' research
Carl Levitin
Moscow. The first official details have emerged in Moscow of ambitious research into 'tectonic warfare' carried out by the former Soviet Union and subsequently by the government of Russia, and involving atte mpts to stimulate 'artificial' earthquakes as weapons of destruction. According to documents obtained by the newspaper Moscow News, two research programmes, the first known as ' Mercury ' and the second as ' Volcano', were aimed at creating new earthquake epicentres by using underground nuclear explosions . Geophysicists are aware that impending earthquakes may be triggered by underground nuclear explosions . But Western geophysicists remain sceptical about tectonic warfare and have all but abandoned research after two unsuccessful phases of activity in the 1960s and 1980s, says Roger Clark, a lecturer in geophysics at the University of Leeds. Clark is not at all surprised that th e Russians tried to create earthquakes and control their location electromagnetically, however. "This sort of science is very much part of their heritage. We don't think it is impossible, or wrong , but past experience suggests it is very, very unlikely. "

The programme , which was secretly launched by the Communist rulers of the former Soviet Union in 1987, and has been unofficially known to Western geophysicists for several years, is now believed to have been abandoned. It would certainly contravene the terms of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, which Russia signe d at the United Nations in Geneva last month . The Mercury project was launched in the former Soviet republic of Azerbaijan, but came to a halt when the republic became independent. It was superseded by the Volcano project. Three underground nuclear tests are believed to have taken place at sites in Kyrgyzstan.

According to the documents, the Mercury project was launched by a secret decree of the Central Committee of the Communist Party and the Council of Ministers of the Soviet Union. The objective was to "develop a methodology for remote operation on an earthquake epicentre by using weak seismic fields and research possibilities of transferring the seismic energy of an explosion ".

The documents say that the Mercury project involved 22 scientific and industrial organizations, including the Geological Institute of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences in Baku. The remit extended to developing the electronic equipment to be installed aboard space satellites that would control the tectonic weapon. The scientists were given three years to complete research, with testing planned for 1990.

During the research phase, Azerbaijani scientists grew increasingly confident and, according to the documents, were sure that " after [a] nuclear explosion, subterranean energy may accumulate at huge distances from the epicentre and reach massive capacity, after which the next directed explosion can release it all ".

Underground testing began at the town of Batken in Kyrgyzstan, and was directed by lkram Ke rimov , of the Azerbaijan Academy of Sciences. The documents say that scientists detonated an underground nuclear charge and tried to control the direction of seismic energy release d using British-built equipment known as 'system 9690 ' .

A report prepared by the Mozhaisky Military Engineering Institute concluded that the test had been a success. But progress slowed considerably following Azerbaijan's independence from the Soviet Union. This is a mid-1960s promotional flyer for speaking engagements by Julia Brown in the San Jose/Oakland area (Civic Auditorium and Leamington Hotel). It was produced and circulated by groups associated with the John Birch Society and its “Truth About Civil Turmoil” (TACT) network, under the local name “Americans for Civil Harmony.”

Julia Clarice Brown was an African American woman from Cleveland. In the late 1940s she joined the Communist Party USA (CPUSA), initially believing it was a civil-rights organization. After a few months she became disillusioned, contacted the FBI, and from roughly 1951 to 1960 served as a confidential informant (not a formal FBI employee or “undercover agent”). The FBI compensated her for information on Communist activities in the Cleveland area and later confirmed this publicly, while stressing that her subsequent political statements were her own and did not represent the Bureau.
She testified before the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) in 1962. Afterward she became a full-time paid speaker for the John Birch Society. In 1966 the Society’s publishing arm (Western Islands) released her book I Testify: My Years as an F.B.I. Undercover Agent. In her public talks and writings she argued that the civil-rights movement was heavily infiltrated and manipulated by Communists who were using racial grievances as a wedge for revolution. She specifically criticized Martin Luther King Jr. on these grounds. Some researchers have noted that her earlier private statements to the FBI and to magazines were more moderate about Communist influence in organizations such as the NAACP than the claims she made after becoming a Birch Society speaker.

The group photo is a widely distributed image from the Highlander Folk School in Monteagle, Tennessee, taken during its 25th-anniversary gathering over Labor Day weekend in 1957. Highlander was a progressive labor and civil-rights education center founded by Myles Horton; it trained many activists (Rosa Parks had attended an earlier session there). It was not a Communist Party institution, though it was repeatedly attacked as a “Communist training school,” investigated, and closed by Tennessee authorities in 1961 amid Cold War pressure.
The photo was turned into billboards, postcards, and flyers by opponents of the civil-rights movement. Numbered figures typically identified are:
•  1 – Martin Luther King Jr.
•  2 – Abner Berry (Communist Party)
•  3 – Aubrey Williams (Southern Conference Educational Fund)
•  4 – Myles Horton (Highlander director)
Rosa Parks is also visible in the original scene. The image was used to imply that King was attending a formal Communist training session and that the movement was under Communist direction.
Historical context
This flyer is a classic example of 1960s right-wing literature that framed the entire civil-rights movement as a Communist conspiracy. The FBI under J. Edgar Hoover did conduct extensive surveillance of King and other leaders, believing certain advisors (notably Stanley Levison) had Communist ties. Hoover publicly denounced King and authorized aggressive counterintelligence measures. Mainstream historians and later assessments have concluded that while there was some Communist interest in and influence around the movement, the movement itself was not Communist-dominated or controlled.
The flyer’s language (“RED DECEPTION,” “fomentation of civil turmoil,” the offer of a booklet titled “VIOLENCE or REASON?”) is typical of the John Birch Society’s messaging at the time. The specific event dates (Aug. 23 and 26) and the San Jose address place it in the mid-to-late 1960s, when Brown was actively touring for these groups.

I’m not disputing the idiom’s conventional meaning. I’m disputing your inference about what MY use of it communicated in this context.

You yourself described the idiom as PRETENDING the other person has insisted. That word is crucial. There is a difference between (1) seriously implying that someone did insist, and (2) humorously acting AS IF they had insisted. A mock concession necessarily invokes the concept of insistence; it does not necessarily communicate that any insistence actually occurred. Unless your “Yes” meant only the theatrical pretense, it conflated two different things. And if it DID mean only the pretense, that qualification is exactly what your answer omitted.

Look at what he actually said: “If I were going to be clear on the topic I’d have to spend 3 or 4 paragraphs on H1-B visa fast tracking…” That was his hypothetical statement about the effort it would take HIM to elaborate. It wasn’t an insistence that I do anything, and it wasn’t even a declaration that he intended to write the paragraphs. My response, “Well, if you insist🫠,” playfully acted as though he was volunteering to write them. The attached image shows a dying man wishing he had spent MORE time arguing online. The joke is that writing several more paragraphs in an online political argument would be an absurd use of one’s life. The meme is not incidental decoration: it tells the audience how to interpret the words.

What real pressure, specifically, was I conceding to? He had not demanded that I do anything; he was merely considering an explanation HE would have to write. That fact alone does not rule out a metaphorical concession, but it makes the context of the joke especially important. “Well, if you insist” was a mock invitation to go ahead and make the effort, simultaneously ridiculing that effort. I was not claiming that he had demanded the opportunity or that I had yielded to a demand. The imagined insistence was the joke’s premise, not my assertion about the preceding post.

This isn’t some meaning I privately invented after the fact. EnglishClub’s entry on “if you insist” explicitly notes a humorous use: someone merely offers another drink, and the reply is “Well, if you insist.” The person offering the drink hasn’t insisted. The responder jokingly constructs insistence as an excuse to accept. This is a publicly documented use of the very same idiom, including “well,” in the absence of any actual insistence. It demonstrates that the conventional expression can operate as playful make-believe rather than a sincere report of pressure. The situations aren’t identical, but the relevant rhetorical mechanism is: jokingly inventing an insistence that the addressee did not actually make. The conventional expression is being used, not discarded.

There’s scholarly support for taking context seriously, too. Kaltenböck and Keizer, “Insubordinate if-clauses in FDG: Degrees of independence” (Open Linguistics, 2022), specifically mention “if you insist” among semi-fixed expressions that can express deprecation or disapproval, and explain that such expressions’ precise interpretations depend on linguistic or situational context. That is strikingly relevant to a response paired with a meme plainly disapproving of more time spent arguing online. The academic point isn’t that the idiom loses its established sense; it’s that identifying its words does not finish the pragmatic analysis.

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s entry on implicature makes the general distinction explicit, using an ironic description of someone as a “stable genius”: an utterance can retain conventional linguistic meaning without the speaker actually communicating the ordinarily associated implication. This is a general point about irony, not a study of this exact sentence. But it directly challenges the rule your replies appear to rely on: “because the idiom normally evokes insistence, the speaker necessarily implied real insistence.” Irony can deliberately evoke a proposition WITHOUT putting it forward as true. Recognizing what is being play-acted is not the same as believing it happened.

I grant that my follow-up “I wasn’t using it in the conventional meaning” was an imprecise way of putting this. More accurately, I was using a conventional expression for an ironic, nonliteral purpose. Without the recognizable idiom the joke wouldn’t work. So I’m not asking my private intention to override English; I’m asking you to interpret familiar English using the publicly visible context, including the conditional statement, the emoji, the meme, and the fact that the proposed action was his, not mine.

Notice what I am NOT asking you to concede. I’m not claiming that “if” magically erases the idiom; that “well” changes its dictionary definition; that nobody could notice the pretense of insistence; or that the words can never be read as mock capitulation. I concede all of those conventional features. I am asking for the narrower point your answers have evaded: did I communicate that he REALLY had insisted, rather than jokingly pretend he was insisting? “Readers get the conventional sense first” does not answer that, because readers can recognize an idiom and recognize its ironic use in the same breath.

So please separate the two propositions and answer them explicitly:

A. My remark rhetorically cast him AS IF he were insisting, for comic effect. That is true.

B. My remark communicated AS A FACT that he HAD insisted, or that I was genuinely yielding to pressure from him. That does not follow, and the public context strongly points against it.

The word “imply” itself can cover more than one kind of suggestion, so the distinction matters. Someone can rhetorically insinuate a fiction as part of a joke without asking an audience to accept it as a real-world proposition. You might reasonably say I “implied insistence” in the very loose sense of playing an insistence scene for laughs. That is compatible with my point, not a refutation of it. What I was denying, and what you should assess, is an implied claim of ACTUAL insistence. Your formulation “conceding to pressure that wasn’t there” makes that distinction essential: is “conceding” part of the mock performance, or are you claiming the communication was genuine?

So please answer the narrower question directly: Given the conditional he wrote and the deathbed meme I attached, did my post convey to a reasonable reader that he ACTUALLY insisted, yes or no?

If no, please say so explicitly: “No, you didn’t imply that he actually insisted; you jokingly framed him as if he had. My original unqualified ‘Yes’ should have made that distinction.” If yes, identify the public evidence for that interpretation and explain why the visibly ironic one is inadequate. I’m not asking you to abandon the idiom’s conventional meaning. I’m asking you to correct the inference you drew from it.

❖ 4 MARCH 2008 · THE ONE THEY DID TRY

A Derg officer was sentenced to death for bombing market towns from the air. Read which towns. Then what was never charged at all.

⚖️ THE CASE
Federal High Court, the Special Prosecutor against Legesse Asfaw and others, judgment 4 March 2008, file 03116. Indicted 3 May 2001. Twenty-three defendants, most of them air force pilots. Five were in the room.

He was a founding member of the Derg, survived its purges, ran the party's organisational affairs, and by 1988 commanded in Tigray.

🕯 WHAT HE WAS SENTENCED FOR
Ordering the indiscriminate bombing of undefended localities — Chila, Wukro and Hawzien.

Hawzien, 22 June 1988. Africa Watch, two years after: high explosives and cluster bombs from the bombers, machine guns and rockets from the helicopters. "One of the most savage on record."

Its own finding was a minimum of a thousand men, women and children deliberately killed.

🔊 AND HIS VOICE, IN THE COURT RECORD
The Mengistu trial ruling carries a radio archive: Legesse Asfaw announcing at the Addis Ababa City Council, for the Derg, that ነፃ እርምጃ would continue — and reassuring the kebeles they would not be held accountable for it.

❖ NOW THE PART THIS THREAD IS FOR
Those three towns are in Tigray. The literature calls him the Butcher of Tigray. That verdict is Tigrayan dead, tried.

Africa Watch again, on the 1984 resettlement: about six hundred thousand moved out of the famine north — Wollo, Tigray, Gondar — and it "is estimated to have killed at least 50,000" of them.

The Special Prosecutor had a team for exactly that: forced relocation and misuse of food aid. The penal code offered the charges. Scholars of these trials record that no prosecution ever followed.

‖ A court established who bombed Hawzien, and sentenced him for it.
‖ Nobody was ever charged for the trucks, and that is the whole argument.

#Derg #Ethiopia #Amhara

12 AM Top-of-the-Hour News

Democrats scored major Senate victories across the country, flipping seats in several traditionally Republican states.: “In the Lone Star State, we just took back Texas. James Tallarico ended a thirty-year Democratic drought. They also picked up seats in Michigan, South Carolina, and Kansas, where a Democrat hasn't won a Senate race in nearly a century. In Maine, Troy Jackson ousted Republican. Susan Collins, who's been in the Senate for 3 decades, and Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown is heading back to the Senate after defeating Republican Jon Husted. This is your victory, Stacy Lynn, Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

The race for Alaska governor is still undecided. Democrat Jonathan Kreis Tomkins is leading at 49 percent. Newsnations Nancy Loo:: “For now, neither Mary Peltola or Senator Dan Sullivan have enough votes to avoid a ranked choice runoff. Republican incumbent Senator Sullivan believes the Double Dan ballot scandal had an impact at the polls, and early returns have shown nearly 3600 votes for Daniel J. Sullivan, the retired school teacher who's come to be known as Decoy Dan. ”
Kreiss-Tomkins falls short of fifty percent, ranked-choice tabulation will decide the winner."

Coalition-building talks have started in Israel after last week’s elections.: “Betsimo pale hola swami flago kgamartishanimekave. ”
Israeli President Isaac Herzog says the doors are wide open to all factions and parties.  Herzog says he's keen to listen and share ideas and find creative solutions to prevent another election.
Herzog accepted the certified results of the election, dealing a blow to prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu's effort to discredit the vote.
Herzog has already met with representatives of the parties elected to parliament.

In Southern California the Los Angeles mayor's race is still being counted. NewsNation’s Kimberly Cheng: “Experts say later arriving ballots tend to come from younger, more liberal voters, a constituency that Rahman has courted throughout her campaign. About a third of ballots still need to be tallied, though the final results could take days. ”
Council member Nitia Raman  is carrying a 2-percent lead over incumbent Karan Bass with about 63-percent of the vote counted.

Canadian authorities said that multiple grizzlies may have attacked a mother and daughter who were found dead in British Columbia.
Family members reported Jenny Balcarras and her daughter Selah Reed missing on Sunday. Their remains were found Monday.
Authorities have imposed a curfew on the Bella Coola community while they search for the animals involved in the deadly mauling. The area is known for having a large population of grizzly and black bears.
A group of 20 elementary students and teachers were attacked last year in the same area. One adult and three children were seriously injured in that attack.

The cruise ship that stranded its passengers in Cambodia has gone back out to sea.: “Only the crew members of the MV Odyssey are still aboard. About half of the 200 passengers are still in Cambodia figuring out what to do next. The other half have returned home or gone on to other countries. They were on a 3 year around the world cruise when the ship's US operator pulled the plug last week because it couldn't afford the skyrocketing fuel costs anymore. There are reports a creditor may have taken over the ship's management and is sailing it to Singapore, Michael Wallace, Worldwide News Network. ”

With open enrollment underway, the Federal Trade Commission is issuing a warning about potentially misleading health insurance ads and scams.
The agency says some companies who promise comprehensive plans actually provide limited benefits and services.
Other companies offer medical discount cards instead of healthcare insurance.
Ads impersonating the government and reputable insurance companies have also appeared on the internet.
The FTC urged people to be cautious about calls, texts, social media messages and online search results.

Yes, I think much of the anti-AI sentiment has been funded by doomer billionaires like Jaan Tallinn, Dustin Moskovitz, Elon Musk, and Sam Bankman-Fried, who have given roughly $500 million to date to a network of doomer NGOs.[1] 

These organizations promote the idea that if advanced AIs are developed without sufficient safeguards, they will inevitably drive humanity to extinction. (As a prominent doomer book puts it: "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies.")[2]

These billionaires were also early investors in Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI. All of those companies see themselves as the only ones sufficiently high-minded and capable of developing "safe" or "aligned" AI.

So these firms are currently lobbying Congress to pass legislation that would impose a de facto ban on open-source and open-weight frontier AI development.

As is no doubt a happy accident, this regulatory moat would also make them fabulously wealthy, as it will help protect them from their startup and Chinese competitors, most of whom will not be able to afford to climb the high regulatory barriers that proprietary AI firms are currently constructing.

So I think that anti-AI doomers are a mix of true believers (who sincerely believe that advanced AI will likely kill everyone) and cynical rent-seekers (who look forward to the massive profits they will earn as a result of their regulatory moat).

Economists have named this combination of unlikely bedfellows working together to impose authoritarian paternalist laws the "Bootleggers and Baptists" strategy.[3]

The name is derived from the history of alcohol Prohibition. Pro-prohibition politicians received financial support and volunteer muscle from both sincere anti-alcohol teetotalers (the Baptists) and smugglers (the bootleggers) who made hefty profits from selling black-market booze.

As we speak, Anthropic is currently spending millions lobbying Congress to ban frontier AI development.[4]

One of the doomer NGO cutouts, the Foundation for American Innovation—which recently received over $1 million in funding directed by Moskovitz and Tallinn—is planning lawfare against the firms who offer uncensored models.[5] [6]

Their long-term plan is to impose a global AI surveillance, censorship, and control regime restricted to Anthropic and perhaps a few other US-based crony firms.[7] [8]

Priscilla[a] and Aquila[b] were a first-century Christian missionary married couple described in the New Testament. Aquila is traditionally listed among the Seventy Disciples. They lived, worked, and traveled with the Apostle PAUL, who described them as his "fellow workers in Christ Jesus" (Romans 16:3).[1]

Priscilla and Aquila are described in the New Testament as providing a presence that strengthened the early Christian churches. Paul was generous in his recognition and acknowledgment of his indebtedness to them (Romans 16:3–4). Together, they are credited with instructing Apollos,[2] a major evangelist of the first century, and "[explaining] to him the way of God more accurately" (Acts 18:26). They were forced from their home during the persecution under Claudius.

It is thought by some to be possible, in light of her apparent prominence, that Priscilla held the office of presbyter.[3] She also is thought by some to be the anonymous author of the Epistle to the Hebrews.[4]

New Testament references
They are mentioned six times in four different books and by two different human penman (Paul and Luke)[5] in the New Testament. They are always named as a couple and never individually. Of those six references, Aquila's name is mentioned first only twice: and one of the times on account of it being Paul's first encounter with them, probably through Aquila first.

Acts 18:2–3: "There he became acquainted with a Jew named Aquila, born in Pontus, who had recently arrived from Italy with his wife, Priscilla. They had left Italy when Claudius Caesar deported all Jews from Rome. Paul lived and worked with them, for they were tentmakers just as he was."
Acts 18:18: "Paul stayed in Corinth for some time after that, then said good-bye to the brothers and sisters and went to nearby Cenchrea. There he shaved his head according to Jewish custom, marking the end of a vow. Then he set sail for Syria, taking Priscilla and Aquila with him."
Acts 18:26: "When Priscilla and Aquila heard him preaching in the synagogue, they took him aside and explained the way of God even more accurately."
Romans 16:3: "Give my greetings to Priscilla and Aquila, my co-workers in the ministry of Christ Jesus."
1 Corinthians 16:19: "The churches here in the province of Asia send greetings in the Lord, as do Aquila and Priscilla and all the others who gather in their home for church meetings."
2 Timothy 4:19: "Give my greetings to Priscilla and Aquila and those living in the household of Onesiphorus."
Note: This is not KJV; in the KJV, Acts 18:26 lists their names as "Aquila and Priscilla" making the count three and three.

The couple
Paul staying in the house of Saints Aquila and Priscilla by Jan van de Venne, 17th century: Paul is at left, writing a letter; Priscilla is at right, spinning, and her husband Aquila is in the background, working on the loom.[6]
Priscilla and Aquila were tentmakers as was Paul.[7] Priscilla and Aquila had been among the Jews expelled from Rome by the Roman Emperor Claudius in the year 49 as written by Suetonius. They ended up in Corinth. Paul lived with Priscilla and Aquila for approximately 18 months. Then the couple started out to accompany Paul when he proceeded to Syria, but stopped at Ephesus in the Roman province of Asia, now part of modern Turkey.

In 1 Corinthians 16:19, Paul passes on the greetings of Priscilla and Aquila to their friends in Corinth, indicating that the couple were in his company. Paul founded the church in Corinth.[8] His including them in his greetings implies that Priscilla and Aquila were also involved in the founding of that church. Since 1 Corinthians discusses a crisis deriving from a conflict between the followers of Apollos and the followers of Cephas (possibly the apostle Peter), it can be inferred that Apollos accompanied Priscilla and Aquila when they returned to Corinth. This happened before 54, when Claudius died and the expulsion of the Jews from Rome was lifted.

In Romans 16:3–4, thought to have been written in 56 or 57,[9] Paul sends his greetings to Priscilla and Aquila and proclaims that both of them "risked their necks" to save Paul's life.

Tradition reports that Aquila and Priscilla were martyred together.[10][11]

Vietnam looks to Israel’s hi-tech industry for opportunity as diplomatic ties at a high - interview
Israeli ambassador Yaron Mayer told the ‘Post’ that Jerusalem-Hanoi relations were at an all-time high.
By DANIELLE GREYMAN-KENNARD
FEBRUARY 1, 2026 09:33
Updated: FEBRUARY 1, 2026 16:22
While Israeli diplomacy undoubtedly has become more complex since the October 7 massacre, the relationship between Jerusalem and Hanoi has flourished, according to Israeli Ambassador to Vietnam Yaron Mayer.

“The conflict has naturally raised concerns but did not dominate bilateral engagement,” he told The Jerusalem Post in a recent interview. “Diplomatic dialogue remained professional, respectful, and focused on cooperation. Long-term partnerships were not disrupted.”

“Vietnam maintains a balanced stance, supporting a two-state solution while continuing to value Israel as a top-tier technological partner,” he added.

Mayer, who is also Israel’s ambassador to Laos, has worked for more than a decade in Israeli diplomacy. He previously served as ambassador to Myanmar and Nepal.

Mayer said he has devoted much of his time to developing bonds on a local level. Celebrating his first Vietnamese New Year, which fell on his seventh month in the country, he joined a kindergarten class to learn how to make traditional Vietnamese Trung, a square cake made of sticky rice, green beans, and meat.

Mayer, whose mother was a famed artist born in London, also reflected on both the challenge and the beauty of learning to write a traditional word under the guidance of a calligrapher in Hanoi. The Chinese script, commonly hung on the walls of Vietnamese homes to bring good luck, was demonstrated by a local man who taught him how to write the word “AN,” meaning peace.

Vietnam boosts Israel ties with tech cooperation, tourism push
The relationship between the two countries is at an all-time high, he said, citing recent accomplishments, such as the signing of the free-trade agreement in 2023. Trade is projected to exceed $4 billion by the end of 2026, he added.

Israelis might be able to travel to Vietnam without a visa in the not-too-distant future, Mayer hinted, adding that it would be a natural next step following Hanoi’s 2023 decision to extend e-visas to 90 days.

The new direct Arkia flight from Tel Aviv to Vietnam indicates that Hanoi is investing heavily in attracting Israeli tourists, he said. Last year, at least 50,000 visitors entered Vietnam with their Israeli passports, and the Vietnamese Tourism Ministry hopes to attract 300,000 Israeli travelers by 2030, he added.

Mayer said a plan was in place to increase cooperation in technology transfer, smart agriculture, climate resilience, and digital innovation within the next five years.

Much of Israel’s environmental and agricultural technology is already being employed by Vietnam, he said. The gold standard of Israeli drip irrigation is now being scaled to address water shortages and efficient irrigation in various regions, he added, and it was being used successfully in many rural parts of the country.

Perhaps because Vietnam only recognized Israel in 1993, Mayer said he was pleasantly surprised by the depth of interest in Israeli innovation across Vietnamese institutions. There is strong demand not only from the private sector, he said, but also from provincial governments and universities.

Vietnam is eager for the opportunity to benefit from Israeli technology, and there are many opportunities for Israelis, Mayer said.

He cited strong interest from Israeli start-ups and said the embassy has begun hosting “matchmaker” events, such as the Israel Technology Connection, to link Israeli start-ups with Vietnamese provincial leaders.

FPT, one of Vietnam’s largest hi-tech and pharmaceutical companies, was one of several to benefit from the work of the embassy and opened the doors to its first Israel office a few weeks ago, Yoram Noar, the head of FPT’s Israel branch, told the Post.

The new office will focus on furthering the company’s interests in the fields of artificial intelligence, cyber, and education, he said.

“I urged the ambassador to focus on the hi-tech industry to see if we could bring the Israeli companies from the hi-tech industry into Vietnam to see if we could do joint ventures,” Noar said. “We focused on hi-tech because Vietnam has great potential, and Vietnam wants to show a growth of about 10% a year, so [Hanoi] thought Israel could be a good model of how to promote [economic and hi-tech] activities.”

Last month, the Hai Phong Center for Innovation and Application of Science and Technology hosted an event that focused on Israeli technology in agriculture and water resources.

More efforts are now being made to help Israel navigate the Vietnamese paperwork, and this would remain an ongoing focus, Mayer said.

A year has passed since President Kim Dae-jung and North Korean leader Kim Jong-il held the first-ever summit meeting between North and South Korea.

Bavarian Deputy Premier Hubert Aiwanger Found Dead at 55 in Berlin Hotel

Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria’s deputy premier and economy minister, was found dead on Wednesday in a Berlin hotel room, aged 55. (The reports described him as Bavaria’s deputy premier and economy minister, and gave his age as 55.) Police said the room was in Berlin-Mitte, giving a more specific location than the broader description of a Berlin hotel. The reports did not identify the hotel by name. The cause of death was not immediately known. Police and prosecutors opened an inquiry to determine both what caused his death and the circumstances surrounding it. Their stated task also includes examining whether another person may have been culpable. Authorities offered no additional information about the investigation.

The accounts establish the reported location and the start of an official inquiry, but they do not provide a conclusion about how Aiwanger died. The cause was described as unclear at the time of reporting, and the authorities had not supplied further investigative details. The inquiry therefore covers more than identifying a cause: it is also intended to clarify the surrounding events and consider possible responsibility by a third party. Those are stated aims, not findings about what happened. The available reporting does not specify the methods used by police or prosecutors, the evidence they examined, or a timetable for their work. It reports only that the two authorities began a probe and gave no further details. Deutsche Welle likewise characterized the circumstances as unresolved. That description is consistent with the reported lack of an immediate cause and the ongoing inquiry, rather than an announcement of a result.

Aiwanger had travelled to Berlin for the planned opening of an office for his party, according to a report attributed to Bild. He missed that event because he was feeling unwell, the same account said. Bild also reported that police later found his body at the hotel. The report links the missed event and the later discovery in the sequence it describes, without supplying further detail about the interval between them. The stated purpose of the trip was a party-office opening, while the inquiry concerns the cause and circumstances of his death. The reporting does not say that the event itself explains what happened. No further account of Aiwanger’s movements in Berlin appears in the listed information. The police and prosecutors also declined to provide additional investigative detail in the reports.

Aiwanger held several political roles in Bavaria: he was deputy premier, economy minister and chair of the Free Voters party. The Guardian also described him as the party’s head and Bavaria’s economy minister. The Free Voters were part of the Bavarian regional government as a junior partner to the Christian Social Union, which was led by Markus Soeder. This places Aiwanger’s party within the state administration, but not as the leading party in the coalition described. Aiwanger had led the Free Voters’ Bavarian branch since 2006. Under his leadership, the party entered the state government for the first time in 2018. These dates describe two different milestones: his leadership of the regional branch began in 2006, while the party’s first entry into government came in 2018. The information does not give the size of the party’s vote or the number of seats it held in the Bavarian legislature.

The party’s reach in state government did not extend to winning enough seats to enter Germany’s federal parliament, according to the reported account. The contrast is between participation in Bavaria’s regional administration and the absence of the required federal parliamentary qualification. That distinction matters when describing Aiwanger’s political position: his reported government responsibilities were in Bavaria, while the Free Voters had not secured the seats needed for the federal parliament. The facts provided do not quantify their support at either level. Aiwanger’s roles therefore connected a state-level governing partnership with leadership of a party that had not qualified for federal representation. This summarizes the institutional context reported, without implying that one position caused or explains the other. The accounts identify the Christian Social Union as the senior partner in the Bavarian government and Soeder as its leader. They do not provide further information about the government’s work or any succession arrangements following Aiwanger’s death.

Soeder responded to Aiwanger’s death by describing it as an absolute tragedy. He also said people were deeply shocked and voiced concern for Aiwanger’s family and children. Those remarks are the reported public response from Bavaria’s premier; the facts do not identify additional official statements or actions. Nor do they describe any administrative decisions made after the news emerged. German media reported that Aiwanger had two children and lived with his partner. That information provides a limited account of his family circumstances, rather than a fuller description of his private life. Soeder’s expressed concern specifically included Aiwanger’s family and children, while the media report identified two children and a partner. The reporting does not provide further details about them.

Aiwanger had also faced national controversy in 2023 over reports concerning an antisemitic pamphlet said to have been written when he was a 17-year-old schoolboy. The reported allegation concerned his authorship of the pamphlet, not a finding stated in the facts here. Aiwanger denied that he had written it, while acknowledging that he had possessed one or perhaps a small number of copies in his school bag. These are distinct parts of his reported response: a denial of authorship and an acknowledgment of possession. He apologized over the affair but did not resign, according to the account. The facts do not describe the wider consequences of the controversy or its effect on the party’s standing. The episode is relevant as part of the reported background to Aiwanger’s public career, but it does not provide evidence about the circumstances of his death. The reported inquiry into his death remains a separate matter with its cause not immediately clear.

The reports present three different kinds of information: the discovery of Aiwanger’s body, the official inquiry, and background on his political and personal life. The discovery is attributed to police, while the party-event account and later finding are attributed to Bild. The authorities’ stated purpose is to clarify the cause and circumstances and to rule out possible culpability by another person. No result or further details from their work were given in the reports. The political background describes Aiwanger’s roles in Bavaria, the Free Voters’ place in the regional government and their lack of sufficient seats for Germany’s federal parliament. It also records his leadership dates and the party’s first entry into the Bavarian government. The available information thus establishes his age, the reported place of discovery and the inquiry’s stated scope, while leaving the cause of death unresolved in the accounts. The reporting also records Soeder’s response and a limited set of biographical details, without providing further investigative findings.

text:
Thank you, 44th District.

When I stepped into this race, I did it because I love our community and believed I had something to offer. I wanted to listen, to serve, and to give people a voice.

While this is not the outcome we worked and hoped for, I accept the result and congratulate April Berg. My prayer is that she will serve the people of the 44th District with wisdom, integrity, and a willingness to listen to every part of our community.

I'm disappointed. We put our hearts into this. But alongside that disappointment, I feel so much gratitude.

To everyone who voted for me, thank you for your trust. To everyone who donated, knocked on doors, put up a sign, shared a post, or encouraged me on a hard day, thank you. You gave your time, your resources, and your heart to something we believed in together.

To my family, especially my husband, thank you for walking through this with me. You saw the long days and late nights, and your love and support carried me through more than you know.

To Doug Roulstone and every volunteer and canvasser who gave their evenings and weekends, thank you. To Chris Elder and Sherri Larkin, thank you for sharing this journey. I'm grateful we had the opportunity to stand together for our community.

One of the greatest gifts of this campaign has been meeting people willing to share their lives with me. Parents worried about their children. Families trying to make ends meet. Small business owners working hard to keep their doors open. People who simply wanted to know that someone was listening.

I heard you. I will carry those conversations with me.

Throughout this journey, I've held onto these words: "His promise is my purpose."

My faith was never a guarantee that I would win an election. It is what gives me the courage to step forward, trust God with the outcome, and keep walking when the path looks different than I hoped.

And I want you to hear this clearly: I'm not done.

We still have work to do. Families need relief. Parents deserve a voice. Our communities deserve safety, and the people of Washington deserve accountability from their government.

I still believe Washington is worth fighting for. This campaign has only strengthened that belief.

I don't know exactly what the next chapter looks like, but I intend to help write it. I hope you'll stay involved, keep speaking up, and join me in the work ahead.

Thank you for standing with me, praying with me, and believing in me. It has been an honor to be your candidate.

Our voices still matter. Our purpose remains. And I'm just getting started.

God bless you, and God bless Washington.

#VoicesUp #RestoreWashington

text:
𝐃𝐄𝐀 𝐆𝐀𝐕𝐄 𝐁𝐀𝐂𝐊 𝐂𝐑𝐈𝐒𝐓𝐀𝐋 𝐒𝐓𝐀𝐑𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐆’𝐒 𝐒𝐓𝐎𝐋𝐄𝐍 𝐒𝐀𝐕𝐈𝐍𝐆𝐒 — 𝐀 𝐂𝐎𝐔𝐑𝐓 𝐒𝐀𝐈𝐃 𝐒𝐇𝐄 𝐃𝐄𝐒𝐄𝐑𝐕𝐄𝐒 𝐍𝐎 𝐈𝐍𝐓𝐄𝐑𝐄𝐒𝐓

In October 2020, Rochester police raided an apartment tied to Cristal Starling’s then-boyfriend, a suspected drug dealer. They never proved a single charge against him that day, but they found $8,040 she had saved to open her own food truck — and walked out with the cash, her personal car, and her work vehicle. “𝘐 𝘩𝘢𝘥𝘯’𝘵 𝘥𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘺𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨,” Starling said. She never had to — because she was never arrested and never charged with a crime.

Her boyfriend wasn’t convicted either. A jury acquitted him of every charge in November 2021, leaving the government with no crime, no conviction, and no case against anyone. By then Rochester police had already handed Starling’s money to the DEA through a federal program called equitable sharing, which lets local departments pocket up to 80 percent of what they seize by routing it through Washington. 𝐒𝐡𝐞 𝐡𝐚𝐝 𝐧𝐨 𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐲𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐩𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 — and the DEA told her the money was gone for good, permanently forfeited without her ever stepping in front of a judge.

The Institute for Justice took her case anyway, and in August 2023, nearly three years after the raid, the Second Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the default judgment outright. The judges ruled that a woman never charged with a crime was entitled to her day in court before the government could keep her savings. 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐞𝐢𝐳𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐚 𝐣𝐮𝐫𝐲, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐄𝐀 𝐬𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐲 𝐠𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐲 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 in January 2024 — only after first offering to settle for half, an offer Starling flatly rejected.

She got her $8,040 back. What she never got was a single dollar for the three-plus years she spent without it. “𝘐’𝘮 𝘪𝘯𝘤𝘳𝘦𝘥𝘪𝘣𝘭𝘺 𝘩𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘺 𝘵𝘰 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘮𝘺 𝘮𝘰𝘯𝘦𝘺 𝘣𝘢𝘤𝘬, 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘐 𝘢𝘭𝘴𝘰 𝘥𝘦𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘱𝘢𝘪𝘥 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘵,” Starling said at the time. In July 2025, a federal judge in the Western District of New York sided with the government instead, ruling she hadn’t “substantially prevailed” — because the DEA could theoretically seize the same money all over again. 𝐍𝐨 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭. 𝐍𝐨 𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐲’𝐬 𝐟𝐞𝐞𝐬. 𝐍𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥.

Institute for Justice senior attorney Rob Johnson didn’t soften what that ruling means for the next Cristal Starling: “𝘠𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘥𝘢𝘺’𝘴 𝘳𝘶𝘭𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘨𝘪𝘷𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘨𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘢 ‘𝘨𝘦𝘵-𝘰𝘶𝘵-𝘰𝘧-𝘧𝘦𝘦𝘴 𝘧𝘳𝘦𝘦’ 𝘤𝘢𝘳𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘯𝘭𝘺 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘧𝘦𝘪𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘢𝘣𝘶𝘴𝘦,” Johnson said. Starling and her lawyers are appealing again, still fighting the same government that took her savings, her cars, and three years of her life — and still hasn’t paid for any of it.

𝐂𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐧𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐫𝐨𝐤𝐞 𝐚 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐥𝐚𝐰. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐡𝐞𝐥𝐝 𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐲 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐧’𝐭 𝐩𝐚𝐢𝐝 𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐚 𝐝𝐢𝐦𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐢𝐭.
